claims.text: An ML-trained molecular-dynamics protocol combined with thermodynamic integration can determine melting temperatures and fusion, volume-change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
The target materials are solid-state high-entropy alloys with disordered atomic configurations under ambient conditions.
Interatomic potentials trained on DFT data can be used in ML-enhanced molecular-dynamics simulations of these alloys.
Systematic temperature ramping and thermodynamic integration can be coupled to ML-enhanced molecular dynamics to characterize melting.
Binary or simpler alloy systems can serve as initial calibration benchmarks for the simulation parameters.
Evolution of atomistic configurations and structural order parameters indicates the onset of melting and the solid-to-liquid transition.
ML interatomic potentials capture complex multielement interactions across the relevant temperature range.
Thermodynamic integration during molecular dynamics quantifies free-energy changes.
Melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting can be extracted from the calculated free-energy changes.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties can be derived from the continuous potential-energy landscape generated by the ML model.
The proposed approach is expected to predict melting temperatures and fusion parameters within approximately 5–10% of experimental and ab initio benchmarks.
The proposed approach will significantly reduce computational cost relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
Calorimetry, thermal analysis, and dilatometry provide experimental benchmarks for melting temperature, fusion thermodynamics, and volume change, respectively.
The approach is applicable to high-entropy alloys with moderate to high chemical complexity.
Predictive accuracy may diminish for compositions or dynamical behavior not represented adequately in the training data.
Predictive accuracy may diminish for systems with extremely subtle phase-transition phenomena.
Extrapolating ML potentials beyond their training compositions and temperature ranges may produce errors greater than 10% in some systems.
Sensitivity to thermodynamic-integration parameters may produce errors greater than 10% in some systems.
The approach is falsified if its predicted parameters consistently differ by more than 10% from both experimental measurements and full ab initio molecular-dynamics benchmarks.
